newsitem.title: MEXICO: Televisa Q1 results give mixed picture.
newsitem.headline: Televisa Q1 results give mixed picture.

text.p: Confusion about management changes at Mexican media conglomerate Grupo Televisa SA may have cleared for now, but analysts on Thursday still scratched their heads about the company's fundamental outlook.

Televisa's first quarter loss of 197.45 million pesos, or 0.21 pesos on a per-share basis, dismayed some analysts and investors who had expected the company to return to profitability after Mexico's recent economic crisis.

The loss was narrower than the loss of 492.55 million pesos during the same period of 1996, but a disappointment compared to a Reuters survey of three industry analysts that had forecast a quarterly profit of 0.24 pesos per share.
"It was a bad result. This company still hasn't turned things around," said a Mexico City analyst who wished to remain anonymous.
Investors did not seem to have been impressed either. Televisa's benchmark CPO (ordinary) shares fell 2.32 percent on the Mexican stock exchange.
Other analysts, however, applauded the results, saying they suffered from one-time financial charges and adding that it was only a matter of time before the company began making money again.
"People's expectations were too high. The numbers were good, but people were disappointed anyway," said Francisco Rivero, an analyst at Valores Finamex in New York.

The company issued its results the same day its shareholders elected a new chairman of the board, Emilio Azcarraga Jean, the 29-year-old son of the late chairman at the company Emilio Azcarraga Milmo.

Azcarraga Jean's replacement of former chairman Guillermo Canedo White at the top came faster than expected, but analysts said Azcarraga was surrounded by an experienced management team, including Canedo White as president of the new executive committee.

The main focus of concern in the quarterly report was Televisa's core television business. It reported an 8.8 percent increase in television sales compared to the same quarter of 1996, but lost market share to rival TV Azteca.
Televisa said it had an average of 67.7 percent of the total TV audience during the quarter, down from 68.0 percent during the last quarter of 1996.
"The results confirmed that Televisa is still losing market share. And TV is its bread and butter," said the Mexico City analyst.

Televisa's new head of operations, Jaime Davila, told analysts during a conference call on Thursday that Televisa plans new programming in late summer to beat back Azteca, especially in the Mexico City market.
Some analysts played down the market share news.
"Televisa has almost completely stabilized its market share loss," said Martin Lara, an analyst at Caspian Research in Mexico City.
Analysts said the quarterly results were partly hurt by non-recurring items such as 50.9 million pesos in severance payments and an unusually high tax charge of 65.5 million.
